idiom_name: begin/rescue SpecificError with an empty body; Kernel#suppress for the named-block form
implementation_notes: Ruby's rescue clause is the local structure: `begin ... rescue SpecificError; end`, a method-level rescue, or the expression-level `rescue Modifier` (`File.delete(path) rescue nil`) are the mute in its various sizes, and only the named exception class keeps it honest. ActiveSupport ships the documented named-block form, `suppress(Errno::ENOENT) { ... }`, which 'blocks and ignores any exception passed as argument if raised within the block' - use it inside Rails applications and the begin/rescue form elsewhere, always with the narrow class and a comment.
code_sketch:
# core: narrow rescue, documented
begin
  lockfile.delete          # may already be gone
rescue Errno::ENOENT
  # documented: absence is the desired end state
end
# ActiveSupport / Rails: named suppression
suppress(Errno::ENOENT) { lockfile.delete }
pitfalls: A bare `rescue` or `rescue => e` without a class catches StandardError and silently hides NoMethodError/NameError-class bugs; always name the class.
Rescuing Exception (rather than StandardError) also traps Interrupt and SystemExit, making the process unresponsive to SIGINT and shutdown.

The rescue modifier applies to a whole expression: in a compound assignment the other parts' failures are muted too, so keep it on the single call and prefer the block form when the call is not the entire expression.
